title: Data and Schema Evolution
learning_outcomes: Explain how data and schema evolution affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from database schema evolution to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on data and schema evolution in api versioning and lifecycle management. You will connect database schema evolution to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Data and Schema Evolution matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying database schema evolution deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “Data and Schema Evolution” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Data and Schema Evolution
content_blocks.code:

content_blocks.expected_output: A version strategy communicates the contract boundary; deprecation needs a timeline, consumer evidence, and migration documentation.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Database schema evolution”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Expand-and-contract migrations” and “API and event schema compatibility”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Compatibility is a consumer property; deprecations need evidence, communication, and a migration path. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating data and schema evolution. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Database schema evolution” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Data and Schema Evolution with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating data and schema evolution as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “Data and Schema Evolution” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
